Mine is Pork Schnitzel.

  1. Get a pork loin or get cut pork filets.
  2. Cut the loin into filets if you didn't get it pre-cut. Thickness will factor into the size of each piece of schnitzel. I prefer a half inch as it makes it easier to...
  3. Pound the filets flat with a meat tenderizer. Try to not massacre it into mush. Salt and pepper the meat. Easy does it.
  4. Grab two large ziploc bags, gallon or larger. Pour about 5 cups of flour in one. 5 cups of bread crumbs, the smashed up kind not the cubes, in the other.
  5. Grab a large, wide bowl. Grab 3-4 eggs. Some milk. Egg yolks and milk in the bowl. Egg shells go in the garbage. Mix it up and create an egg wash.
  6. Put the pounded filets, one at a time, in the flour. Cover them and soak up the moisture with the flour.
  7. Dip the flour coated filets in the egg wash. Get them all wet. Immediately transfer them to the bread crumbs. Coat them with the bread crumbs until the whole filet is coated and the wash is soaked up.
  8. Rest the filets in the fridge while you grab some oil, vegetable is fine, and heat a few ounces up in a wide skillet, pan, wok, whatever.
  9. Fry the filets until they're crispy and a little bit browned. Put them in the oven at around 350 degrees on a broiler pan if you have one. This will finish cooking the meat, further crisp the coating, and drain off the excess oil. Don't burn them.
  10. Eat with a little spritz of lemon. Some heathens add gravy. Leftovers are great with some mayo.

Some tips:
1. melt the butter in the baking dish, that way you mess up one less dish and don't have to grease the baking dish.

  1. you don't have to mix the dry ingredients in a separate bowl, I never do. Just add them to the top of the wet ingredients, the batter is thick enough where they should just stay on the top. Mix them together as much as you can before you fold them into batter. I only have to clean one mixing bowl and the baking dish.

  2. add in a half cup of something for variety. Some of my favorites are Reese Peanut Butter chips, chocolate chips, and pecans. Just keep in mind that when you use a toothpick to check for doneness if you hit one of the chips it will still be wet like it isn't done. Also, the additonal mass will increase cooking time. Wait until the brownies start to pull away from the sides of the dish and there is a good crack down the middle. They are chewier (and better) the next day if they make it that long.

What is "Sous Vide" and Why should you consider cooking with this technique?

This always struck me as a gimmick to sell hardware. Just try braising, it's much easier and once you get hang of it, pretty awesome.

Basically a braise combines the best of both worlds, sauté and marinade. Take something like a cheap, tough cut of steak. Even grilled to perfection, you'll still be chewing that thing for a good 30 minutes.

Instead, take some good fat (I like pork shoulder) or cooking oil (safflower is good) and sear both sides, get a real nice browning on it. Once it looks good, drain off any excess oil (this is important) and stir in some combination of broth, wine and water. I keep chicken broth and white wine in my kitchen so that's what I use. Add enough liquid to cover whatever you're cooking about halfway, you don't need to submerge it. Get it to a low simmer, then put a lid on it for the better part of an hour.

Play around with the cooking times a bit until you know when the liquid is about ready to condense into a delicious sauce. Take the lid off to speed up the process if you must, but it will reduce the infusion of flavor to a degree. You can also add a bit of cornstarch to bulk it up. That $5 strip steak can be fork tender in a rich sauce without some crazy TV infomercial setup.
